justifications.c1: Independent per-incident figures well above £5k: ABI's 2023 average burst-pipe claim above £17,000 (Insurance Times, search-confirmed), Zurich's £12,791 average escape-of-water repair, AXA's older £25k; but none is specific to social-housing voids (recorded not found), and Lambeth's £240k/yr is a screen contract, not a loss.
justifications.c2: Insurers 'normally require inspections every 7 or 14 days' with time-stamped reports (IFSEC trade article) and policies specify 7/14/30-day inspections (Federato, US vendor); no social-landlord policy wording or void-check frequency from the tender was visible.
justifications.c3: Paid workarounds are documented and priced: SafeSite weekly logged inspections and a monitored void alarm from £35 a week (search-confirmed, vendor), Lambeth's £240k-a-year VPS screen contract and Void Clerk of Works roles; but no insurer is shown accepting sensors in place of physical inspections, so removal of that cost is unproven.
justifications.c4: Insurer unoccupancy conditions exist (Masonic Mutual, COSIC, Oxford forms; titles only) and the FOS blog confirms insurers decline escape-of-water claims in unoccupied homes on condition breaches (search-confirmed), sometimes overturned; FOS covers consumers and small firms, and no social-landlord block-policy wording was found.
justifications.c5: Voids Manager (Home Group, £50k–£55k) and Property Officer (Voids) adverts show void-budget responsibility, but void security is bought by formal contract award or tender (Lambeth, Find a Tender), which slows a direct sale.
justifications.c6: Void-security firms already serve this exact site type and sell alarms and logged inspections (VPS social-housing sector, SafeSite, Clearway), and Eddisons sells RemoteZone remote monitoring from its insurance arm; strong channel, though these firms are also competitors.
justifications.c7: Willingness to pay is proven (SafeSite £35/week alarm, Secom £485/month, Lambeth £240k/yr), but sensor-based vacant-property monitoring already exists (Eddisons RemoteZone, Corps Security Beespace, WCCTV); the claimed gap (leak and temperature proof accepted by insurers) is unevidenced.
justifications.c8: Off-the-shelf parts exist (Milesight WS301 door contact $52, Codepoint CS1040 tilt sensor $49.99) and battery-plus-cellular is the accepted architecture, but the multi-sensor hub (temperature, leak rope, PIR, vibration, mains loss, LTE-M) implies a BOM above £50, and LTE-M and leak-sensor prices were not gathered.
justifications.c9: Landlords already pay weekly (£35/week, i.e. well over £100 per site per year) and insurers want time-stamped inspection records, but each void ends on re-letting and no insurer accepts sensor logs as the record, so the subscription case rests on redeployment.
justifications.c10: Insurer loss data (ABI, Zurich), ombudsman material (FOS blog), council documents (Clackmannanshire voids hit by burst pipes; Wolverhampton 630 burst pipes in council homes), a regulator void dataset (SHR) and a Mumsnet thread (title only).

weakest: No insurer is shown accepting sensor data in place of 7- or 14-day physical inspections, so the product may add cost rather than replace the inspection it targets.
